item.title: Entering the agentic era of AI in drug discovery
item.description:
Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 19 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02295-x

Agentic AI systems are reshaping drug discovery, and the convergence of agentic AI with laboratory automation is enabling the design of self-driving laboratories that transform the design–make–test–analyze cycle into a closed-loop, adaptive workflow. Here, we discuss these advances and the potential that agentic AI holds for drug discovery.

item.title: A chemigenetic endogenous Ras activity biosensor for live-cell pharmacology
item.description:
Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 19 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02276-0

Here the authors present a biosensor for measuring endogenous Ras in live cells, based on HaloTag and the fluorogenic JF635 dye, and they use it to report location-specific inhibition profiles of distinct Ras pathway drugs.

item.title: Living circuit boards built by printing bacterial transistors
item.description:
Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 17 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02300-3

Electronic circuit boards carry out different operations on the basis of the configuration of their components. Now, equivalent biological circuits are engineered that compute functions on the basis of the spatial arrangement of different bacterial strains printed on a surface.

item.title: Photoproximity labeling of c-Myc reveals SLK as a cancer-specific co-regulator
item.description:
Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 13 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02284-0

A photoproximity-labeling approach maps cancer-specific partners of the c-Myc oncoprotein, revealing that the kinase SLK binds and stabilizes c-Myc, drives tumor growth and offers a new strategy to target this long-‘undruggable’ driver of cancer.

item.title: A dual assault on KRAS
item.description:
Nature Chemical Biology, Published online: 12 August 2026; doi:10.1038/s41589-026-02283-1

KRAS(Q61) mutant oncoproteins drive cancer through defective GTP hydrolysis. A study now shows that small molecules can restore catalytic activity while simultaneously shifting KRAS toward its inactive state, identifying an unexpected strategy to target previously untreatable KRAS mutants.
